intro: Rachmaninoff plays his Sérénade, Op. 3 No. 5, which he wrote at nineteen. A few soft notes around F lead into a waltz, which fades to near silence before a final loud chord.

sections.label: A · Sostenuto, turning figures over F
sections.mNote: Sostenuto: small turning figures over a left-hand F.

sections.label: B · Tempo di Valse
sections.mNote: Bass notes and offbeat chords accompany the melody

sections.label: Coda · pppp chords, final ff chord
sections.mNote: Chords marked pppp lead to a final chord marked ff.

cues.title: Opening, Sostenuto
cues.text: The left hand begins on F, pp, in a slow 3/8. Small turning figures move around that note before the right hand enters with chords.
cues.evidence: Sérénade, first version (1892), collected piano edition, p. 284: Sostenuto, 3/8, pp, left-hand F and turning figures. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/df/IMSLP39537-PMLP05664-Rachmaninoff-Op3-Serenade-Ver1892.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tchaikovsky interview, November 1892
cues.text: In November 1892 Rachmaninoff read an interview in which Tchaikovsky named him among the outstanding young composers. Delighted, he sat down at the piano and added this Sérénade to his planned set of four pieces. Gutheil published all five the following February.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker’s notes to Hyperion CDA66081 describe Tchaikovsky’s November 1892 interview, Rachmaninoff’s addition of the Sérénade and publication in February 1893. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6690_66081

cues.title: Tempo di Valse
cues.text: At Tempo di Valse, in 3/8, a bass note and offbeat chords set up the waltz accompaniment. The melody turns around neighbouring notes and extends the turning figures of the opening into a longer line.
cues.evidence: First-version score, pp. 284–285: Tempo di Valse in 3/8, bass-and-chord accompaniment and turning melodic figures. Dominik Rahmer’s Henle commentary (2022), at bars 103–104, records differences between the composer’s recording and the printed first version: https://www.henle.de/media/76/20/d9/1697725714/1491-1697725714-sync.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Victor recording sessions, New York, 1922
cues.text: Victor’s ledgers record five takes of the Sérénade in New York, three on 1 November 1922 and two on 4 November. The first four were destroyed, and the fifth was issued on Victor 66129 and 816. For 1 November the ledger names the piano: “Steinway piano, style B-211833.”
cues.evidence: DAHR matrix B-27110 lists takes 1–3 (1 November 1922) and 4–5 (4 November), New York, takes 1–4 destroyed and take 5 as master on Victor 66129 and 816, and quotes the Victor ledger note of 1 November: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/800001056/B-27110-Serenade

cues.title: Final chords
cues.text: The waltz thins to chords marked ppp, then pppp. A final fortissimo chord follows, held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: First-version score, p. 287, final two systems: ppp and pppp chords, then a final ff chord under a fermata. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/df/IMSLP39537-PMLP05664-Rachmaninoff-Op3-Serenade-Ver1892.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From Sostenuto to Tempo di Valse
transitions.from: A · Sostenuto, turning figures over F
transitions.how: The opening returns repeatedly to F, the dominant of B♭ minor. After chords marked ppp, a short rising run leads the piano into Tempo di Valse. The left hand starts its bass-and-chord pattern, and the small turning figures become the melody of the waltz.
transitions.evidence: First-version score, p. 284: recurring F, ppp chords, rising run and Tempo di Valse. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/df/IMSLP39537-PMLP05664-Rachmaninoff-Op3-Serenade-Ver1892.pdf

transitions.title: Waltz bass stops before final chord
transitions.to: Coda · pppp chords, final ff chord
transitions.how: The waltz bass stops and the piano moves into descending chords, marked ppp and then pppp. Small turning figures continue above the bass. The piece ends on a single ff chord under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: First-version score, p. 287, final two systems: descending soft chords, turning figures and the final ff fermata. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/df/IMSLP39537-PMLP05664-Rachmaninoff-Op3-Serenade-Ver1892.pdf

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original (1892) version of the Sérénade, as played by the composer in 1922; performing text not identified
fields.note: Wikipedia’s list of the composer’s recordings labels the 4 November 1922 recording the 1892 version, and the 1940 revised version was published only in 1940 (Henle). IMSLP’s page says No. 5 was revised in 1922; the Henle report documents the revised text as Charles Foley’s 1940 edition, so that remark is not followed. Henle also states that the composer’s own recording diverges from the printed notation of the original version in many places. Henle does not identify which composer recording it means; the cited original score is therefore not assumed to be a literal transcript of the 1922 performance.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: DAHR’s approved take 5 is dated 4 November 1922; takes 1–3 were made on 1 November. The Archive filename and the RCA register give the same date for the reissued track.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives New York for every take; no studio is named.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Victor is the original label; the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Victor 66129 (10-inch single-faced) and Victor 816 (10-inch double-faced, with Bizet’s Minuet); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
fields.note: The Victor numbers and the CD set are separately documented. The disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: DAHR names the matrix, takes and issues. The link between that take and this digital file rests on the RCA register (which names the matrix and take for the CD track) and the uploader’s CD identification; no waveform or run-out comparison with the disc was made.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
fields.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Victor 66129 and 816, recorded 1922).
fields.note: DAHR’s catalogue records for Victor 66129 and 816 give a publication date of [1922], and an Internet Archive digitisation of Victrola 66129 gives 1922; both are catalogue-derived years, not release days. The 1925 Victor catalogue lists the Serenade (Op. 3, No. 5) coupled with the Minuet from L’Arlésienne, which establishes publication no later than 1925 independently of the session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
